title: "Lab 12: Multilevel Models I"
date: April 22, 2026
---




## Overview

-   Today we will learn how to fit multilevel models in `brms`.

-   In previous labs, each parameter applied to everyone included in the model. However, this method ignores within-person variation. 

-   To allow for individual differences, we can use multilevel modeling.

-   Instead of using a separate intercept for each observation, the multilevel approach uses teh method of partial pooling to model a distribution of intercepts. 

## Multilevel Models

To illustrate, let's load in the `TDF.csv` data, along with the `tidyverse` and `brms` packages. 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse); library(brms)
d1 <- read_csv("TDF.csv")
```
:::


::: columns
:::: column

Previously:

$$\omega_i \sim Normal (\mu_i, \sigma)$$

$$\mu_i = a + b \times hc_i$$

$a \sim N(66.5, 2)$

$b \sim N(1, .5)$

$\sigma \sim Exp(.25)$

::::
:::: column

Now: 

$$\omega_i \sim Normal (\mu_i, \sigma)$$

$$\mu_i = a + b \times hc_i$$
$a \sim N(\bar{a}, \sigma_a)$

$\bar{a} \sim N(66.5, 2)$

$\sigma_a \sim ???$

$b \sim N(1, .5)$

$\sigma \sim Exp(.25)$

::::
:::



## Multilevel Models

We can allow for random intercepts using the `(1 | ID)` syntax, where `ID` is the clustering variable. 

* This is the same syntax used by `lmer` and `glmer` for multilevel models.

For our height and weight example, our formula looks like this: 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
brm_form1 <- Weight ~ HeightC + (1 | Name) 
```
:::


## Priors

Use `get_prior` to see how parameters are represented.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
get_prior(brm_form1, d1, 
          family = gaussian(link = "identity"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
                 prior     class      coef group resp dpar nlpar lb ub tag
                (flat)         b                                          
                (flat)         b   HeightC

  student_t(3, 0, 7.4)        sd            Name                  0       
  student_t(3, 0, 7.4)        sd Intercept  Name                  0

```


:::
:::



## Priors

As we see in the `class` column, we have a new parameter class labelled `sd`. This is the prior for the standard deviation of intercepts.

* Recall: intercept = predicted weight for average height

* We may expect some individual variability. We will try an `Exponential(.5)`. 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
prior1 <- prior(normal(66.5, 2), class = "Intercept") +
          prior(exponential(.5), class = "sd") +
          prior(normal(1, .5), class = "b") +
          prior(exponential(.25), class = "sigma")
```
:::


## Prior Predictive Simulation


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
predict1 <- brm(brm_form1, d1,
                family = gaussian(link = "identity"),
                prior = prior1, cores = 4, sample_prior = "only")
```
:::


## Prior Predictive Simulation

Our choice of `sd` prior affects the width of the band of predicted observations, so we want to make sure this makes sense.

* `method = "posterior_predict"`: plot the distribution of predicted observations

* `re_formula = NULL`: include all cluster effects


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
conditional_effects(predict1, method = "posterior_predict", re_formula = NULL)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Multilevel_Models_I_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::




## Model Fitting


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
m1 <- brm(brm_form1, d1,
          family = gaussian(link = "identity"),
          prior = prior1, cores = 4)
```
:::


## Model Results

Notice that even for this relatively simple multilevel model, estimation is not as efficient as with other models. We need to be cautious to run enough iterations for the inferences we want.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
summary(m1)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

## Model Results

* $\bar{a}$ is the overall mean intercept.

* The **random effects** (`ranef`) are individuals' deviations from the mean intercept.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
individual_intercepts <- ranef(m1)$Name[,"Estimate",]
ggplot() + geom_density(aes(x = individual_intercepts))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Multilevel_Models_I_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=960}
:::

## Another Example


Let's now look at the more complicated `langauge.csv` example from lecture. 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
d2 <- read_csv("language.csv")
```
:::


We want to estimate index variables for both task type and learning group type, and we want individuals to have random intercepts.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
brm_form2 <- bf(sumscore|trials(nitems) ~ a + b + c,
                a ~ 0 + factor(tasktype),
                b ~ 0 + factor(group),
                c ~ (1|ID), nl = TRUE)
```
:::


## Priors

Remember that we fit a multilevel binomial model for these data.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
get_prior(brm_form2, d2,
          family = binomial (link = "logit"))
```

## Priors

It is a long list, but we can simplify matters by specifying the same priors for each set of index variables. There is no need to specify priors for each `coef` (unless you want to!). Here, we use the priors from lecture.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
prior2 <- prior(normal(3, .5), class = "b", coef = "Intercept", nlpar = "c") +
          prior(normal(0, .5), class = "b", nlpar = "a") +
          prior(normal(0, .5), class = "b", nlpar = "b") +
          prior(exponential(2), class = "sd", nlpar = "c")
```
:::


## Model Fitting & Results


::: {.cell messsage='true'}

```{.r .cell-code}
m2 <- brm(brm_form2, d2,
          family = binomial (link = "logit"),
          prior = prior2)
```

## Adding On

We can set multiple types of random effects. For example, we could consider the random effects of both persons and items.

For example:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
d3 <- read.csv("language item.csv")
brm_form3 <- bf(response ~ a + b + c + d,
                    a ~ 0 + tasktype,
                    b ~ 0 + group,
                    c ~ (1 | ID),
                    d ~ 0 + (1 | item), nl = TRUE)
```
:::


## Priors

Now, we can set separate `sd` parameters for two different `group` values: `ID` and `item`:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
get_prior(brm_form3, d3, 
          family = bernoulli(link = "logit"))
```

## Priors

Again, we'll use the same priors that we did in lecture.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
prior3 <- prior(normal(0, .5), class = "b", nlpar = "a") +
  prior(normal(0, .5), class = "b", nlpar = "b") +
  prior(exponential(1), class = "sd", nlpar = "c") +
  prior(normal(3, .5), class = "b", coef = "Intercept", nlpar = "c") +
  prior(exponential(2), class = "sd", nlpar = "d")
```
:::


The following model takes **much** longer to run: **BE WARNED**!!!


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
m3 <- brm(brm_form3, d3,
          family = bernoulli(link = "logit"),
          prior = prior3, cores = 4)
```
:::

## Model Results

As we can see, the variation of items is much larger than the variation of individuals!


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mean_ind3 <- ranef(m3)$ID[, "Estimate", ]
mean_item3 <- ranef(m3)$item[, "Estimate", ]

ggplot()+
  geom_density(aes(x = mean_ind3), color = "red")+
  geom_density(aes(x = mean_item3), color = "blue")
```

![](Multilevel_Models_I_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){width=960}

## Activity

1. Modify `m3` so that items are treated as a fixed effect rather than a random effect. Compare the output to that of `m3`. 

2. Modify `m2` so that `tasktype` is a random effect rather than a fixed effect. How does this affect model run time and convergence? How does this affect the interpretations that you make?
